To goggle means to stare at something with your eyes opened very wide — often so wide that your eyes appear to be bulging slightly outward — because you are shocked, amazed, or can't believe what you're seeing.

It's not just looking. It's not even just staring. It is a very specific kind of stare — the one where your eyes go as big and round as they possibly can, almost as if they're about to pop out of your face.

Think of a moment when someone sees something so unbelievable that their jaw drops and their eyes go wide. Maybe a child seeing a towering six-layer birthday cake for the first time. Maybe someone opening a letter and discovering they've won a million dollars.

That moment — those big, round, almost cartoonishly wide eyes — is exactly what "goggle" describes.
The Two Things It Captures at Once

What makes "goggle" a powerful word is that it captures both things simultaneously:

  1. A physical appearance → the eyes are wide, round, and bulging.
  2. An emotional state → the person is shocked, stunned, or amazed.

When you use "goggle," you don't have to separately say "his eyes went wide" and "he was shocked." The single word does both jobs at once.

To goggle at something/someone is the most natural way to use it.

  • She goggled at the price tag on the dress.

(She stared wide-eyed in shock at how expensive it was.)

  • The tourists goggled at the giant statue.

(They stared with wide, amazed eyes.)

  • He goggled when his friend walked in wearing a banana costume.

(His eyes went wide in disbelief.)

You can also describe the eyes themselves as goggling:

  • His eyes goggled at the sight of so much food.

(His eyes widened and seemed to bulge in amazement.)

Goggling is almost always caused by one of these feelings:

  • Shock — something completely unexpected just happened.
  • Disbelief — you're seeing something but your brain is struggling to accept it.
  • Amazement — something is so impressive or extraordinary that it overwhelms you.
  • Confusion — something is so strange or bizarre that you just stare blankly.
How It Differs From Similar Words

There are many words for "staring," and each one captures something slightly different. Here's what makes "goggle" unique:

  • To stare — to look at something for a long time. Very general. Says nothing about your eyes or your emotion.
  • To gape — to stare with your mouth hanging open. The focus is on the open mouth, not the eyes.
  • To ogle — to stare at someone in a creepy or overly interested way, often with desire. Has a slightly negative, inappropriate tone.
  • To gawk — to stare in a rude, clumsy, or foolish way, often when you shouldn't be staring (like at an accident).
  • To goggle — to stare with wide, bulging eyes specifically. The unique focus is entirely on the dramatic, exaggerated appearance of the eyes.

So if you want to describe that very specific image of someone's eyes going wide like saucers in surprise, goggle is the precise, perfect word.

"Goggle" is a slightly informal and vivid word. Writers use it when they want to paint a clear mental picture for the reader. It has a mildly comic or exaggerated quality — when you say someone goggled, there's almost a cartoonish image that forms in the mind. Because of this, it fits naturally in storytelling, fiction, and everyday informal speech.
To goggle = to stare at something with wide, bulging, round eyes because you are shocked, amazed, or cannot believe what you are seeing.
